questions.stem: How does a Vision Transformer turn an image into a sequence?
choices: It flattens the image into one long vector of pixels
It splits the image into fixed-size non-overlapping patches, flattens each, and linearly projects it into a token embedding
It uses a CNN to produce tokens
It converts the image to text
questions.explanation: Patchifying is what makes attention tractable: a 224x224 image at 16x16 patches becomes 196 tokens rather than 50,176 pixels, since attention cost grows with the square of sequence length. Each patch is linearly projected to the model dimension, exactly as a word embedding would be.

questions.stem: Why does a ViT need positional embeddings when a CNN does not?
choices: Because images are larger than text
Self-attention is permutation-invariant, so without position information the model would treat the patches as an unordered set
Because patches overlap
Because transformers cannot process colour
questions.explanation: Convolution encodes spatial arrangement structurally — a kernel sees a specific neighbourhood. Attention treats tokens as a set, so shuffling patches would leave the representation unchanged. Positional embeddings restore the geometry that patchifying discarded.

questions.stem: ViTs underperform CNNs when trained from scratch on small datasets. Why?
choices: They have fewer parameters
CNNs build in locality and translation equivariance as inductive biases; a ViT must learn those from data, which takes far more of it
ViTs cannot use augmentation
Attention is numerically unstable at small scale
questions.explanation: A convolution assumes nearby pixels are related and that a feature means the same thing anywhere — assumptions that are correct for images and free. A ViT starts with no such prior, so it needs either large-scale pretraining or heavy augmentation and regularisation to discover them.

questions.stem: What is the class token in a ViT for?
choices: It stores the ground-truth label
A learnable token prepended to the patch sequence whose final representation is used as the whole-image embedding for classification
It marks the end of the sequence
It encodes the patch size
questions.explanation: Borrowed from BERT's [CLS], it gives a position that belongs to no particular patch and can therefore aggregate across all of them through attention. Some later architectures drop it and use global average pooling over patch tokens instead, which works comparably.

questions.stem: What does Swin Transformer change to make ViTs practical for dense prediction?
choices: It removes attention entirely
It computes attention within local windows and shifts those windows between layers, giving linear cost in image size plus a hierarchical multi-scale feature map
It uses larger patches
It replaces the decoder
questions.explanation: Global attention over high-resolution feature maps is quadratic and unaffordable for detection or segmentation. Windowed attention makes cost linear, and shifting the window partition between consecutive blocks lets information cross window boundaries. The hierarchy then plugs into FPN-style heads like a CNN backbone.

questions.stem: How is CLIP trained?
choices: By classifying images into 1,000 ImageNet categories
Contrastively on image-text pairs: matching pairs are pulled together in a shared embedding space and mismatched pairs pushed apart
By predicting the next word of an image caption
By reconstructing masked image patches
questions.explanation: Two encoders, one for images and one for text, are trained so that a photo and its caption land near each other. No fixed label set is ever defined, which is precisely what makes the resulting model able to recognise categories it was never explicitly trained on.

questions.stem: How does CLIP perform zero-shot classification?
choices: It is fine-tuned on each new class
Candidate class names are embedded as text prompts and the image embedding is matched against them, so new classes need only a name
It generates a caption then parses it
It requires one labelled example per class
questions.explanation: Because images and text share an embedding space, classification becomes nearest-neighbour retrieval against text embeddings of the candidate labels. Adding a class costs a string. Prompt wording measurably affects accuracy, which is why prompt ensembling is common.

questions.stem: Which TWO are genuine limitations of CLIP-style zero-shot recognition?
choices: Performance depends heavily on how class names are phrased in the prompt
It reflects the biases and coverage gaps of its web-scraped training data, so fine-grained or specialist categories are often weak
It cannot process colour images
It requires the class list at training time
questions.explanation: Prompt sensitivity and training-distribution coverage are the two practical failure modes. A specialist category absent from web text — a specific industrial defect, a rare species — has no useful text embedding to match against. The class list being needed only at inference is the whole point, not a limitation.

questions.stem: What is open-vocabulary detection?
choices: Detecting an unlimited number of objects per image
Detecting object categories specified at inference by text rather than fixed at training by a closed label set
Detecting text in images
Detecting objects without any training
questions.explanation: A conventional detector has a fixed head sized to its class list; adding a category means retraining. Open-vocabulary detectors align region features with text embeddings, so a new category is a new phrase at inference — enormously valuable when the taxonomy is fluid.

questions.stem: What does self-supervised pretraining such as DINO or masked autoencoding give you?
choices: Labels for free
Strong visual representations learned from unlabelled images, which then need far fewer labels to fine-tune for a downstream task
A complete classifier
Faster inference
questions.explanation: The pretext task — matching views of the same image, or reconstructing masked patches — needs no annotation, so it can consume vastly more data than any labelled set. The learned features transfer, so the expensive labelled data is spent only on adaptation. That economics is why self-supervision matters in practice.

questions.stem: In a masked autoencoder for images, what is the model trained to do?
choices: Classify the masked patches
Reconstruct the pixel content of patches that were hidden from the encoder, forcing it to learn structure and context
Predict the next image in a sequence
Match the image to its caption
questions.explanation: Masking a large fraction of patches — often 75% — and reconstructing them makes the task hard enough to require genuine understanding of object structure rather than local texture copying. The decoder is discarded after pretraining; only the encoder's representation is kept.

questions.stem: How does a latent diffusion model reduce the cost of image generation?
choices: By generating smaller images
By running the diffusion process in a compressed latent space produced by an autoencoder, rather than directly on high-resolution pixels
By using fewer denoising steps only
By generating in grayscale first
questions.explanation: Diffusion needs many sequential denoising passes, and doing them at full pixel resolution is prohibitive. Compressing to a latent roughly 8x smaller per side cuts the work by more than an order of magnitude, with a decoder restoring pixels at the end. That is the key idea behind Stable Diffusion.

questions.stem: What does classifier-free guidance control in a conditional diffusion model?
choices: The number of denoising steps
How strongly generation adheres to the conditioning prompt, by extrapolating between the conditional and unconditional predictions
The image resolution
The random seed
questions.explanation: The model is trained both with and without conditioning, and at sampling the two predictions are combined with a scale factor. Higher guidance follows the prompt more literally at the cost of diversity and, past a point, visual artefacts — the classic quality-versus-fidelity dial.

questions.stem: Why is attention cost a bigger problem for images than for typical text?
choices: Images use more colours
Token count scales with the square of image resolution while attention scales with the square of token count, so resolution enters at the fourth power
Images cannot be batched
Text tokens are smaller
questions.explanation: Doubling image resolution quadruples patches, and quadrupling tokens raises attention cost sixteenfold. That compounding is why plain global attention is impractical for high-resolution vision and why windowed, hierarchical or linear-attention designs dominate dense prediction.

questions.stem: You have 5,000 labelled images of an industrial part. Which TWO transformer-based approaches are sensible?
choices: Fine-tune a self-supervised or ImageNet-pretrained ViT backbone rather than training one from scratch
Use a CLIP or DINO backbone as a frozen feature extractor and train a small head on top
Train a ViT from random initialisation on the 5,000 images
Use classifier-free guidance to generate labels
questions.explanation: Five thousand images is far too few to teach a transformer the inductive biases a CNN gets for free, so the pretrained representation is the asset. Fine-tuning adapts it; freezing it and training a head is cheaper still and often competitive at this data scale. Guidance is a generation control, not a labelling method.

questions.stem: What practical advantage does a hybrid CNN-transformer backbone offer?
choices: It removes the need for pretraining
Early convolutions supply locality and efficient downsampling while later attention layers model long-range relationships, combining the strengths of both
It uses less memory than either alone
It eliminates positional embeddings
questions.explanation: Convolutions are efficient and carry useful priors at high resolution where attention is most expensive; attention excels once the sequence is short and global context is what remains to be modelled. Putting each where it is strongest is why hybrid designs are common in production backbones.

questions.stem: A ViT pretrained at 224x224 is fine-tuned at 384x384. What must be handled?
choices: The patch size must change
The positional embeddings were learned for a fixed grid of patches and must be interpolated to the new grid size
The class token must be removed
The optimiser must be changed
questions.explanation: A larger input at the same patch size yields more patches, so the learned position table no longer matches the grid. Bicubic interpolation of the positional embeddings to the new layout is the standard fix and is built into most implementations. Skipping it silently scrambles spatial information.

questions.stem: What makes attention maps attractive but unreliable as explanations?
choices: They are too small to read
They show where the model attended, which is suggestive but not a faithful account of what caused the prediction — attention weight is not causal attribution
They are only available during training
They require a separate model
questions.explanation: Attention is one component in a deep stack with residuals and MLPs, and high weight on a region does not establish that the region determined the output. Attention maps are a useful debugging signal; causal claims need intervention-based attribution methods.

questions.stem: Why does a diffusion model need many sampling steps while a GAN generates in one forward pass?
choices: Diffusion models are larger
Diffusion generates by iteratively reversing a noising process, so each step removes a little noise; a GAN's generator maps noise to an image in a single mapping
GANs use more memory
Diffusion requires text conditioning
questions.explanation: The iterative structure is what gives diffusion its stability and sample quality — each step is a small, well-conditioned problem — and it is also why inference is slow. Step-distillation and improved solvers exist precisely to cut the step count.

questions.stem: Raising classifier-free guidance from 3 to 15 makes images match the prompt more literally but look oversaturated and strange. Why?
choices: The model is broken at high values
Guidance extrapolates away from the unconditional prediction; pushed far enough the result leaves the region the model was trained to produce, trading diversity and realism for prompt adherence
The latent space is too small
The random seed changed
questions.explanation: Guidance is an extrapolation, not an interpolation, so large scales move the prediction outside the learned distribution. The artefacts are the signature of over-extrapolation. Practical values sit in a narrow band, and the right one depends on the sampler and model.
